implementation_notes: In Node the pool is a library, not a language feature: generic-pool's createPool({create, destroy, validate}, {max, min, maxWaitingClients, acquireTimeoutMillis, fifo, idleTimeoutMillis}) returns a Promise-based pool whose acquire() resolves with a resource that must be given back through release() - or destroy() when it is broken - and pool.use(fn) wraps acquire/release/destroy around a single callback. The factory's validate runs on borrow only when testOnBorrow is set, and the optional evictor destroys resources idle beyond idleTimeoutMillis. Node's single-threaded event loop removes data races on the free list but not starvation or leaks, so acquireTimeoutMillis and maxWaitingClients are the exhaustion policy.
pitfalls: Every acquire() must be paired with release() in a finally block; an await between acquire and release does not make it safe, it only makes the leak asynchronous and silent.
Released resources are ordinary objects: nothing prevents a stale reference from issuing another query after release, which is the JavaScript form of double-return and corrupts your own invariants.
The evictor and the pool hold timers and open handles - an undrained pool keeps sockets and keeps the process alive, so call drain()/clear() on shutdown.
